title: Gatekeepers, Treasurers and Local Officials
overview: This chapter lists the Levite families (the tribe set apart for religious service) whom David assigned to guard the gates of the planned temple, look after its treasures, and serve as officials across Israel.

parts.label: The gatekeeper families (vv. 1-11)
parts.note: Gatekeepers guarded the temple entrances, opened its heavy gates and protected its valuables, so the list keeps stressing strong, capable men. The text says God blessed Obed-Edom with many sons; whether he is the same man who once sheltered the ark, the sacred chest, in his home is debated.

parts.label: Gates assigned by lot (vv. 12-19)
parts.note: Posts were drawn by lot, young and old alike, so no family could claim the best gate by rank, and ancient Israel often saw drawing lots as a way of leaving a decision to God. The east gate, likely the busiest entrance, got the most guards; some of the gate names are obscure, and scholars are unsure exactly where they were.

parts.label: Keepers of the treasuries (vv. 20-28)
parts.note: Other Levites managed the storerooms of supplies and the 'dedicated things,' valuables given to God, much of it plunder taken in war. Gifts from Samuel, Saul, Abner, Joab and David all ended up in one treasury, which many readers take as a sign that the whole nation's past fed into the temple.

parts.label: Officials beyond the temple (vv. 29-32)
parts.note: Some Levites worked away from the temple as officials and judges, handling both religious matters and the king's business. A large group was placed with the tribes east of the Jordan River, and the chapter dates these records to David's fortieth and final year as king.

think: What does it say about a community when the people who guard the doors and keep the accounts are named and remembered alongside its famous leaders?
